sm.d: The GPU's “workshop”: a replicated unit that executes warps, with its own registers, shared memory/L1, INT/FP32 units and tensor cores. The GB10 has 48; a GB300, 160.

gb10.d: The DGX Spark's SoC: 20 ARM cores and a consumer Blackwell GPU (compute capability 12.1, sm_121, 48 SMs) in the same package, with 128 GB of unified LPDDR5X (~273 GB/s theoretical).

warp.d: A group of 32 threads (lanes) that the SM executes together, receiving the same instruction in the same cycle. It is the GPU's real unit of execution and scheduling.

lane.d: Each of the 32 positions of a warp (index 0–31). Each lane has its own registers; lanes exchange values through shuffles.

simt.d: Single Instruction, Multiple Threads: the GPU's execution model, in which one instruction is applied by the 32 threads of a warp, each on its own data.

divergencia-de-warp.d: When the lanes of a warp take different paths at a branch (if/else), the warp executes the paths in series, with some of the lanes switched off: it loses efficiency.

cta.d: Cooperative Thread Array: a group of up to 1,024 threads that runs entirely on a single SM, shares one allocation of shared memory and can synchronize at a barrier. A kernel launch's grid is made of CTAs.

kernel-gpu.d: A function compiled for the GPU and launched by the CPU as a grid of CTAs; thousands of threads execute the same function on different parts of the data.

warp-shuffle.d: Instructions (__shfl_sync, __shfl_xor_sync…) that exchange register values between the lanes of a warp without going through memory. The basis for reductions and for the fast Hadamard in the EXL3 kernels.

shared-memory.d: Fast memory in each SM, managed by the programmer and visible to all threads of a CTA. ~100 KB per SM on consumer Blackwell (12.x), ~228 KB on Hopper/datacenter Blackwell (public table).

cache-l2.d: A single cache shared by all SMs, sitting between them and the memory (DRAM) controllers. Query its size with torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).L2_cache_size.

acesso-coalescido.d: When the 32 lanes of a warp read consecutive addresses, the hardware merges the requests into a few 32 B (sector) or 128 B (line) transactions. Scattered accesses pull in a whole sector to use a few bytes and can multiply traffic by as much as 8.

ocultacao-de-latencia.d: The GPU's strategy for living with slow DRAM: while one warp waits for data, the scheduler switches, at no cost, to another ready warp. It requires many resident warps (occupancy).

lei-de-little.d: Bytes in flight = bandwidth × latency. It says how many pending reads the chip needs to keep outstanding to sustain a given bandwidth, given the time each access takes.

ocupacao.d: The fraction of the warps an SM can hold that are actually resident. Limited by the resource that runs out first: registers per thread, shared memory per CTA or warp slots.

spill.d: When a thread needs more registers than allowed, the compiler writes the excess to local memory (STL) and reads it back later (LDL), generating extra DRAM traffic.

memoria-local.d: Per-thread private memory used for spills and dynamically indexed arrays. Despite the name, it lives in DRAM (behind the L1/L2), which is why each LDL is expensive.

tensor-core.d: The SM unit that executes an entire block of a matrix product per instruction (MMA), in low-precision formats (FP16/BF16, FP8, FP4…) with FP32 accumulation.

mma.d: A tensor core instruction that computes \(D = A\,B + C\) over fixed-shape fragments, such as m16n8k16 (\(2mnk\) = 4,096 FLOPs per instruction).

mma-sync.d: A synchronous MMA executed by the whole warp, with operands spread across the registers of the 32 lanes. It is the path on consumer Blackwell (SM12x), including block-scaled FP4.

wgmma.d: Hopper's (sm_90) asynchronous MMA, issued by a group of 4 warps (a warpgroup), with operand B read from shared memory.

tcgen05.d: The family of tensor core instructions of datacenter Blackwell (sm_100/103): asynchronous, issued by a single thread, with the accumulator in TMEM. It does not exist on SM12x (GB10).

tmem.d: Memory dedicated to the tensor cores' accumulator on datacenter Blackwell, used by tcgen05.mma. Absent on consumer Blackwell.

gate-de-capability.d: A piece of code that queries the GPU's compute capability (or family) to choose a path: native kernel, fallback or error. Exact equalities such as == (12, 0) tend to exclude the GB10 (12.1).

ptx.d: NVIDIA's stable virtual assembly. nvcc generates PTX; ptxas (or the driver, via JIT) translates it into SASS for a specific GPU. Unsuffixed PTX compiles for equal or higher CCs.

sass.d: The real machine code of a GPU architecture (what the SM executes). An sm_XY SASS runs on GPUs with the same major and minor ≥ Y; with the a suffix, only on the exact CC.

cubin.d: A binary file with the SASS of kernels for one architecture (sm_XY). Several cubins and PTX go together in a fatbin; JIT caches store already-compiled cubins.

fatbin.d: A container with several cubins (SASS for different architectures) and/or PTX. At load time, the driver picks the compatible SASS; failing that, it JIT-compiles the PTX; failing that, it errors out with “no kernel image is available”.

sufixo-a.d: An architecture-specific target (e.g., sm_121a): unlocks instructions exclusive to that CC, such as block-scaled MMA, but the binary runs only on it.

sufixo-f.d: A family target (e.g., 12.0f): features common to the family and compatibility among its members (a 12.0f cubin runs on 12.1).

torch-cuda-arch-list.d: A variable read by torch.utils.cpp_extension to choose the targets when compiling CUDA extensions: 12.1a generates -gencode arch=compute_121a,code=sm_121a. The GLM and DeepSeek recipes use 12.1a.

cuda-toolkit.d: The CUDA compilers (nvcc, ptxas), headers and runtime. cu130 wheels are compiled against CUDA 13.0, the version all three recipes use; the toolkit must know the target (sm_121).

atomics-vetoriais.d: Atomic operations on 16 bytes at once (e.g., atomicAdd on float4, the red.v4 instruction, sm_90+). GLM's E3 uses them so that several experts can add into the same token.

lpddr5x.d: Low-power DRAM (phones, laptops). In the DGX Spark: 128 GB on a 256-bit bus at 8,533 MT/s (≈273 GB/s theoretical), shared by CPU and GPU.

hbm.d: High Bandwidth Memory: stacks of DRAM mounted next to the chip, with 1,024-bit interfaces per stack, used in datacenter GPUs. It reaches terabytes per second (public specification).

modelo-custo-passo.d: \(t_{\text{step}} \approx \sum_i Q_i / B_{\text{eff}} + t_{\text{fixed}}\) and tok/s ≈ τ (accepted drafts + 1) ÷ \(t_{\text{step}}\): the sum of the bytes read per GPU at each decode step divided by the effective bandwidth, plus fixed costs (collectives, launches).

lancamento-de-kernel.d: The request the CPU enqueues on a stream (“run kernel K with this grid and these pointers”). It is asynchronous and costs CPU time; hundreds per decode step add up to fixed cost.

stream-cuda.d: A work queue the GPU consumes in order. Operations on the same stream are sequential; different streams can overlap if there are free SMs.

evento-cuda.d: A marker recorded on a stream that another stream (or the CPU) can wait on. It expresses dependencies between streams without stopping the CPU.

sync-host-device.d: When the CPU needs a value from the GPU (.item(), .tolist(), .cpu(), data-dependent shapes), it waits for the queue to drain; the GPU sits idle until new launches arrive.

uva.d: A single virtual address space for CPU and GPU: a kernel can read or write directly into pinned host memory. On the GB10 the physical memory is also the same.

memoria-pinned.d: Host memory locked in RAM, which the copy engine accesses via DMA. Only copies to/from pinned memory are truly asynchronous; with pageable memory the driver stages the data and the copy becomes synchronous.

escopo-de-memoria.d: The suffix of a PTX load, store, atomic or fence (.cta, .gpu, .sys) that says among whom the promised ordering holds: threads of the same block, of the same GPU, or of the whole system, CPU included. The wider the scope, the more expensive the guarantee.

estagios-de-pipeline.d: How many input slices a kernel keeps in flight in shared memory: with S stages, it loads the next one while it computes on the current one. Each extra stage is one more buffer; with 99 KiB per block on the GB10, TensorFold's chunked KDA Triton kernels ended up with a single one, until they were replaced by a CUDA kernel.
